19821-the-nursery-no-103-july-1875-vol-x:
The Nursery was a monthly magazine for young children, printed in Boston. Number 103, July 1875, is volume eighteen of the run. Its publishers promise coming numbers to make little readers' eyes sparkle. No other magazine, they boast, can take its place with its audience. Canvassers are urged to start work with a will. Subscription selling kept such magazines alive.

Magazines for the very young were a new trade in 1875. Large type, pictures, and short pieces suited new readers. The Nursery came from the circle of John L. Shorey, its publisher. Bound volumes lived in family libraries for years. A single number preserves the era's nursery taste. Stories, verses, and booster talk share its pages.
3821-the-roman-and-the-teuton-a-series-o:
Charles Kingsley delivered these Cambridge lectures on the fall of Rome and the rise of the Gothic peoples. The contents move from the forest children and the dying empire through the human deluge to Dietrich, the Gothic civilizer, and his end. Then come the nemesis of the Goths, the Lombard laws, and the popes. Max Muller, who supplies a preface, remembers Kingsley as a caged lion of a mind, striving for utterance.

Later lectures weigh the clergy and the heathen, the monk as civilizer, and the strategy of providence in history. Kingsley argues with energy and moral heat, favoring the Teuton as a fresh force against a tired empire. Students of the early Middle Ages will find a dated but stirring survey, best read as a Victorian mind wrestling with the birth of Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-fil:
Francesco Filelfo, born at Tolentino on 25 July 1398 and dead at Florence on 31 July 1481, was a humanist whose restless career carried Greek learning into Renaissance Italy. He taught at Padua by eighteen, then at Venice, and in 1419 became secretary to the Venetian consul-general at Constantinople. There he learned Greek under John Chrysoloras, married his teacher's daughter, served the emperor John Palaeologus on diplomatic missions, and gathered a great collection of Greek books.

Back in Italy he taught at Venice, Bologna, and Florence, where quarrels with Florentine scholars and hatred of the Medici forced him out in 1434. At Milan, Filippo Maria Visconti showered him with honours, and under Francesco Sforza he wrote the Sforziad, a Latin epic in sixteen books on Sforza's life. He left Milan in 1474 for a professorship at Rome, closing a life spent between courts, universities, and feuds.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KSFO_KSFO:
Harold Weisberg wrote on February 27, 1968 to a man named Jack in San Francisco. The letter reports his radio appearances on the coast. It also covers Jim Garrison's subpoena of Allen Dulles, the former CIA director, and interviews Weisberg had conducted with men named Hell and Howard.

A subpoena aimed at a former director of Central Intelligence was Garrison at his boldest, and Weisberg followed it closely. The letter mixes the researcher's two lives: broadcasting his case by day, working sources by mail. It preserves both, three weeks into a very public investigation.
nasa-tm-19660006060-waste-management-and:
Extended crewed missions cannot throw waste away, so this report works through waste management and personal hygiene in a sealed spacecraft. Its contents move from the problem itself to techniques of collection and transport. Storage, processing and reclamation, and final rejection each receive a full section. System designs are then built by joining those pieces in different ways.

Personal hygiene closes the plan, from oral care to shaving and showering. Long flights to distant targets were the design case. A crew's health and morale rest on such unglamorous systems working quietly. The report shows mission planning at its most practical, where daily life must be engineered like any engine.
nasa-tm-19660014385-a-comparison-of-two-:
Robert B Owen at Marshall compared two greenhouse models of the Venus atmosphere in a December 4, 1963, report. Cytherean is an older name for Venus and its air. A greenhouse model explains how the air traps heat and makes the surface far hotter than sunlight alone would. Carl Sagan had proposed both the original model and a newer one, Owen notes.

Recent measurements of water vapor, by Spinrad, fit the original idea, Owen reports. The newer model points to surface conditions more extreme than had been suspected. Owen builds his comparison from a survey of the literature. Before any probe landed, models like these were the only guide to the Venus surface.
nasa-tm-19670016747-fundamentals-of-sele:
Koichi Masubuchi and R. E. Keith, of the Battelle Memorial Institute, wrote this report in January 1967 under an Army contract. Distributed through the Redstone Scientific Information Center in Alabama, it surveys what was then known about how adhesive-bonded joints deform and fail. The same questions cover the thin interface where metal meets adhesive.

The survey's first chapter covers theoretical and experimental stress analyses of bonded joints, plus their flow behavior over time. Fracture, and the effects of loading and environment on deformation, get full treatment, as do design and fabrication problems. A second chapter turns to the atom-level mechanisms by which metal-adhesive interfaces deform. The closing chapter draws conclusions and recommends directions for future research. The authors note the survey was written to assist another investigation in the same field.
nasa-tm-19680014424-calculation-of-captu:
John V. Dugan Jr. and James H. Rice of Lewis Research Center, with John L. Magee of the University of Notre Dame, calculated collision rates for ions and polar molecules in this May 1968 report. Their test case was methyl cyanide, a symmetric top molecule written CH3CN. Such collisions react strongly, so their capture rates matter to chemists.

The team computed the capture cross sections with numbers rather than simple formulas. Adding the molecule's rotational freedom changed the results in clear ways. The values fell below the top classical limit but stayed far above the older Langevin values. When the results were combined over energy, they agreed well with what the paper reports from prior work.
nasa-tm-19680024875-an-analysis-of-blade:
Julian L. Jenkins Jr. of Langley Research Center analyzes blade motion stability for articulated helicopter rotors in this May 1968 paper. A fully articulated rotor lets each blade flap and move in lead-lag motion. Jenkins solves the coupled nonlinear equations of motion numerically to judge stability.

Two effects of starting conditions on the divergence limit are examined. He varies where the disturbance begins around the rotor's rotation. He also varies the disturbance size at the critical azimuth angle. Methods to extend the divergence boundary are then tested. Hinge restraint from springs and damping is weighed, as is flapping hinge cant angle. A representative combination of these fixes is also evaluated.
nasa-tm-19720008259-comparison-of-temper:
Herbert J Gladden, John N B Livingood, and Daniel J Gauntner of the Lewis Research Center compared two test worlds in February 1972, as NASA TM X-2477. Their subject was a finned turbine vane cooled by air jets and an air film. One data set came from a still four vane cascade in a laboratory. The other came from a real research gas turbine engine. Designers needed to know if cheap cascade tests told the truth.

The cascade ran gas at heat up to twenty two hundred fifty degrees Fahrenheit. Its pressure reached eighty pounds per square inch. The team recorded average and local metal temperatures in both settings. They then matched the temperature patterns in several ways. Agreement would validate cascade testing for future cooled vane work.
nasa-tm-19720011337-remote-evaluation-of:
Victor L Coles of NASA presented this paper in September 1971 at a forum on interactive bibliographic systems. The forum met at the National Bureau of Standards in Washington. Coles described how NASA judged its own literature search service, NASA RECON. RECON let users at remote consoles search technical literature interactively. NASA wanted steady feedback from the people actually using it. The paper runs to twenty nine pages.

The method was simple and direct. An evaluation form went out with every literature search performed. Users returned their judgments along with the results. The report explains the technique in full. It also presents the findings drawn from those returned forms. The work is an early study of user satisfaction with online searching.
outlines-of-universal-history-designed-a:
George Park Fisher, a Yale professor, designed his Outlines of Universal History as a textbook for advanced pupils and for private reading. In his preface he lists what such a book should do. It should present the essential facts in due order. Those facts should follow the best and latest research. The book should show how events and eras connect. Illustrative incidents should relieve the dryness of a mere summary.

It should also, Fisher insists, be free from sectarian partiality and limit itself to well-established judgments on contested matters. Writing it impressed on him more than ever the unity of history — the great, deeply moving drama still advancing into a hidden future. He hopes that feeling communicates itself to the reader page by page.
podcast-dannyjones-rPyLoTvYqfo:

podcast-joerogan-Ag7GEsPQhFo:

podcast-joerogan-rTKu9wxEFFo:

podcast-tuckercarlson-N3z_kpaLmFo:
Rob O'Neill, the Navy SEAL credited with killing Osama bin Laden, shares shocking stories from SEAL Team 6 with Tucker Carlson. O'Neill's years in the elite unit took him through America's hardest missions. Here he also tells politicians what they should know before starting wars.

O'Neill recounts missions and losses that shaped his view of combat and command. He argues that leaders who never served send troops too easily into long wars. Carlson asks about the bin Laden raid and the fame that followed it. Patriots and the curious get straight talk from the man at the tip of the spear.
quotes-and-images-from-the-tales-and-nov:
Quotes and Images from the Tales and Novels of Jean de La Fontaine gathers the tale-teller's sharpest lines. They stand in alphabetical order. A short life of La Fontaine follows them. He was born on July 8, 1621, at Château-Thierry. His family held a respectable position there.

The extracts warn the reader with a pretty wife to beware the monks as he would guard his life, and hold that above all law is might. Delays are dangerous in love or war, extremes in everything soonest tire, and the god of love and wisdom never agree. We scarcely find good without alloy, the tales conclude, in their worldly, smiling way.

the-lake-of-the-sky-lake-tahoe-in-the-hi:
George Wharton James devoted this volume to Lake Tahoe. The lake lies in the high Sierras of California and Nevada. L. C. Page and Company of Boston published it in 1915. James had written Arizona, the Wonderland and other western books. The subtitle is a contents list in itself. The lake's history, Indians, and discovery by Frémont appear. Legendary lore, various namings, and glacial features follow. Geology, automobile routes, and historic towns come next. Early mining excitements, the steamer ride, and mineral springs fill it out.

The book carries a map and sixty-five plates. A folding panorama is among them. James adds a full account of the Tahoe National Forest and its waters. He dedicates the volume to Robert M. Watson. Bob is fearless explorer, expert mountaineer, and peerless guide. Truthful fisherman, humane hunter, and delightful raconteur follow. The dedication sets the book's hearty, boosterish tone.
